title: Childhood Onset of Anti-N-Methyl-D-Aspartate Receptor Encephalitis Without Teratoma Masquerading as a Psychotic Disorder
journal: Journal of the Korean Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
case_prompt:
A 9-year-old previously healthy girl was admitted to a closed psychiatric ward for acute behavioral problems. Two months earlier, she had mild somatic complaints—including abdominal pain, headache, and eye discomfort—followed a week later by abrupt-onset cessation of verbal expression, strange vocalizations, severe irritability, agitation, and sleep disturbance. She also showed mild bilateral upper-extremity stiffness but had no prior neurological history or family history of psychiatric or neurologic disorders.

In the emergency department, vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel, were unremarkable. Noncontrast head CT showed no abnormalities. She was diagnosed provisionally with psychotic disorder not otherwise specified and started on risperidone, paroxetine, and benztropine, but symptoms worsened, with auditory and visual hallucinations.

Five days later, she was admitted to a child psychiatry unit for presumptive early-onset schizophrenia. Risperidone and then olanzapine were titrated, improving irritability and sleep only slightly; bizarre behaviors and disorientation in time and place persisted. Neurology was consulted. Ten days after admission, brain MRI revealed no parenchymal or cerebrospinal fluid–space abnormalities. Electroencephalography and lumbar puncture were planned but could not be performed because of the patient’s agitation. Given her young age, rapid progression, and poor response to antipsychotics, autoimmune encephalitis was suggested as a possible diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Psychotic disorder not otherwise specified — “There were no abnormalities in her laboratory examinations; therefore, the patient was referred to a psychiatric department with provisional diagnosis of psychotic disorder not otherwise specified.”  
2. Early-onset schizophrenia — “Autoimmune encephalitis was suggested as a possible diagnosis, as she was too young and the disease progressed too rapidly to be considered early-onset schizophrenia, and she did not respond well to standard antipsychotic treatment.”  
3. Vascular disease or intracranial tumor — “Brain computed tomography was performed in the emergency room (ER) to rule out any neurological condition such as a vascular disease or tumor. There were no abnormalities.”  
4. Structural brain pathology (e.g., demyelination, space-occupying lesions) — “Ten days after her initial admission, the patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); however, no abnormalities in the parenchyma or CSF spaces were detected.”
